♻ ☆ Bilingual Language Models Capture Cross-Linguistic Influence in Second-Language Reading
Abderrahmane Issam, Irene E. Winther, Stefan L. Frank
While monolingual language model (LM) surprisal is widely established as a predictor of reading times, it cannot capture the non-native (L2) reading dynamics that are shaped by the reader's first language (L1). In this work, we investigate whether the cross-lingual transfer within bilingual models aligns with human L1-driven biases during L2 reading. We evaluate bilingual models on eye-tracking data of readers from 12 diverse L1 backgrounds reading English texts. To isolate L1-specific transfer, we compare bilingual models trained on an L1 that matches the readers' L1 background to both a monolingual English baseline and bilingual models trained on other L1s. We demonstrate that matching the readers' L1 improves the prediction of L2 reading times. This predictive advantage is concentrated in late-stage eye-tracking measures, modulated by L1-L2 script overlap, and peaks among intermediate-proficiency readers. These findings provide evidence that bilingual LMs capture aspects of cross-linguistic influence, and that such influence is present in L2 reading behavior.
comment: Under review
♻ ☆ Correctness vs Efficiency: Behavior Control with Weight-Space Extrapolation in Code RL NeurIPS 2026
Kunhao Zheng, Pierre Chambon, Juliette Decugis, Jonas Gehring, Taco Cohen, Benjamin Negrevergne, Gabriel Synnaeve
A model trained with an imperfect reward in RL may learn to exploit the reward with undesired behavior. We study a controlled form of this problem in competitive programming. A program may pass small tests while violating the intended efficiency requirement on larger inputs. We construct a family of rewards that progressively relax the efficiency constraint, making the reward increasingly easy to exploit, and train separate policies. This sweep reveals a correctness-efficiency frontier. Relaxing the reward leads to less efficient programs and more resource-limit failures. Stricter rewards suppress these failures but increase correctness failures near the model's capability boundary. This frontier is also reflected in weight space. Interpolating between the resulting models reproduces the same behavioral change. More surprisingly, extrapolation in both directions further amplifies or suppresses it beyond the trained checkpoints. Extensive experiments show that this pattern holds across pure reasoning, tool use, and agentic coding, and at both 32B and 7B scales. This suggests a simple intervention for this form of reward hacking: use a loose reward to amplify the undesired behavior, use the weight-space difference to a strict-reward model as its steering vector, and then extrapolate past the strict model to suppress it.

♻ ☆ Web World Models
Jichen Feng, Yifan Zhang, Chenggong Zhang, Yifu Lu, Shilong Liu, Mengdi Wang
Language agents increasingly require persistent worlds in which they can act, remember, and learn. Existing approaches sit at two extremes: conventional web frameworks provide reliable but fixed contexts backed by databases, while fully generative world models aim for unlimited environments, but the world is constructed primarily through generation, making it harder to maintain a fixed, deterministic global framework and reducing controllability. In this work, we introduce the Web World Model (WWM), a middle ground where world state and ``physics'' are implemented in ordinary web code to ensure logical consistency, while large language models generate context, narratives, and high-level decisions on top of this structured latent state. We build a suite of WWMs on a realistic web stack, including an infinite travel atlas grounded in real geography, fictional galaxy explorers, web-scale encyclopedic and narrative worlds, and simulation- and game-like environments. Across these systems, we identify practical design principles for WWMs: separating code-defined rules from model-driven imagination, representing latent state as typed web interfaces, and utilizing deterministic generation to achieve unlimited but structured exploration. Our results suggest that web stacks themselves can serve as a scalable substrate for world models, enabling controllable yet open-ended environments.

♻ ☆ Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves 0.391 of the Optimum, Past the One-Third Barrier for Packing-Based Analyses
Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju
Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds most language-model tokenisers by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols. How much shortening can this greedy rule lose against the best $k$ merges? Kozma and Voderholzer proved that greedy achieves at least one third of the optimal shortening; the best known upper bound is $(1-e^{-2})/2\approx 0.432$. We show that one third is a barrier for packing-based analyses, which see the optimum only through a pair packing, and we prove that greedy achieves at least $0.391$ of the optimum on every input, with any tie-breaking. The key idea is rule determinism: all copies of a rule of the optimum spell the same letters, so when one greedy replacement destroys three of the optimum's merge points, half a unit can be refunded on each side. A weaker bound, $0.374$, has a short proof that needs no computer; $0.391$ adds a certificate in exact arithmetic. We also show that the worst-case ratio is exactly $3/4$ for two merges and at most $7/12$ for three.

♻ ☆ Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds NeurIPS 2026
Axel Ahlqvist, Richard Guan, Juan-Pablo Rivera, Adeline Kassler, Dmitrii Troitskii, Alexandra Souly, Kai Fronsdal, Robert Kirk, John Hughes
A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. We show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that they compare favorably to spending the extra compute on more audit attempts.

♻ ☆ Polarity Blindness in LLM Safety: A Systematic Study of Negation, Antonym Substitution, and Adversarial Framing
Diego Miguel Lozano, Erik Derner, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Nuria Oliver
Negation remains a persistent challenge for language models across NLP tasks and modalities. We show that this weakness can undermine LLM safety guardrails through a structural vulnerability we term polarity blindness: the failure to recognize harmful intent after polarity-altering linguistic transformations. We study two forms of polarity inversion: grammatical negation and antonym replacement, and use synonym replacement as a polarity-preserving control. We further test whether an adversarial textual wrapper amplifies these failures. Using a 260-prompt benchmark across 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and 3 languages (English, Spanish, Czech), stratified by harmfulness potential and evaluated on a validated 0-5 harm scale, we find that polarity blindness affects most evaluated models, with mean harm scores reaching 4.12 for the most vulnerable model. The effect persists across typologically differing negation systems, suggesting that polarity blindness reflects a broader limitation in semantic robustness rather than a language- or grammar-specific failure.

♻ ★ Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
Fazl Barez, Tung-Yu Wu, Hunar Batra, Gabriele Dominici, Florent Draye, Yanai Elazar, Damiano Fornasiere, Antía García, Abir Harrasse, Riley Harris, Sara Hooker, Michael Lan, Belinda Z. Li, Aaron Maiwald, Narmeen Fatimah Oozeer, Naomi Saphra, Or David Shafran, Adi Simhi, Robert Trager, Shriyash Kaustubh Upadhyay, Ziyu Yao, Yu Zhao, Shay B. Cohen, Mor Geva, Yoshua Bengio, Stella Biderman, Hassan Sajjad
Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.
♻ ☆ LoopWeaver: Weaving Feedback Loops into Hierarchical Generation under Constraints NeurIPS 2026
Yifan Zhu, Guanting Chen, Bing Wei, Haoran Luo
Large Language Models face a multi-objective optimization problem in constrained long-text generation, balancing global structure, local coherence, and constraint satisfaction. We propose LoopWeaver, a hierarchical workflow with two sequential offline preference-optimization stages. Constraint-aware planning produces structured plans, feasibility filtering removes invalid plans, and a shared deterministic reward constructs preference pairs for plan-level and generation-level DPO. At inference time, LoopWeaver remains feed-forward: it generates and revises a complete plan, filters the revised plan, and then generates segments conditioned on the current sub-plan and running narrative. We evaluate the method on four LongGenBench-style structured scenarios across multiple backbones. Results show improvements in both constraint accuracy and text quality across all four open-source backbones. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/cgtaa-cmyk/LoopWeaver.
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 main conference
♻ ☆ AWARE-FX: Auditable measurement of corporate foreign-exchange hedging disclosure
Qi Wang
Corporate annual reports describe hedging through transactional, policy, accounting, and explicit non-use language. This study presents AWARE-FX, the foreign-exchange application of the Auditable Weak-supervision and Aggregation framework, for constructing traceable firm-year disclosure measures. Professional-source retrieval, evidence-state rules, channel classifiers, and top-three aggregation link each score to supporting passages. The application covers 24,909 Hong Kong firm-years from 2008-2025 and 543,527 candidate snippets. Evaluation combines weak-label held-out tests, three-seed encoder comparisons, a 2023-2025 temporal test, calibration diagnostics, selective prediction, and a stratified 300-snippet audit coded by one researcher. The paired temporal tests do not detect statistically significant differences between FinBERT and ModernBERT. The negation-aware lexicon has higher broad-task audit F1 than strict-gate FinBERT and Qwen3-8B, demonstrating that learned models do not uniformly improve on domain rules. At 80% temporal coverage, retained-sample F1 increases by 0.050-0.077, although the study does not measure human review time or deployment impact. Reproducible Qwen3-8B results show substantial variation across evidence channels. Linked exposure associations provide exploratory external validation, with sensitivity to the multiple-testing family. The scores measure detected hedging disclosure rather than hedge notional or causal effectiveness. The contribution is an evaluated measurement workflow with inspectable evidence and explicit validation limits. Independent duplicate annotation and retrieval-recall assessment remain necessary for stronger reliability claims.
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures, 13 tables. Revised and shortened version of v1. Preprint: not peer reviewed
♻ ☆ How Much Do Structural Tools Help Small Coding Agents? A Pre-Registered Scale Study of Code Localization
Saurav Bellam
Code-graph and embedding tools are routinely added to LLM coding agents on the premise that they supply repository structure the model lacks. We report a pre-registered study of how much such tools help off-the-shelf agents localize the code an issue requires changing and how the benefit varies with model size. Nine open-weight models (Qwen3 0.6B to 32B, Gemma 4 E2B to 12B) run one fixed localization harness on 500 held-out SWE-bench tasks under four tool sets (grep only; plus embedding search; plus code-graph tools; both) and a placebo arm whose structural tools return random entities, with five sampled seeds per condition: 170,500 episodes under hypotheses, tests and claim criteria frozen before the runs. The tools raise canonical function Acc@10 by +0.06 to +0.10 for the Qwen3 models up to 14B and the two small Gemma 4 models, by +0.03 at 32B (a near miss after correction), and not at all for Gemma 4 12B, which rarely submits; the gain is larger for small models than for the largest model in both families. The placebo shows that the gain is caused by what the tools return rather than by having them, and that random tool output harms two small models. The pre-registered claim that a 4B model with tools matches a 32B model without them fails. Secondary analyses show that the embedding index, not the code graph, carries the gain; that the gain replicates on tasks created after every model's release and survives a shell harness, thinking mode, FP8 serving and a file-level metric that output formatting cannot inflate; and that it is mostly exposure: the tools show the gold code more often. Injecting the gold code directly explains the size trend. A 32B model already finds the code without the tools, so they add little exposure, while small models act on a shown answer less often (conversion 0.09, 0.24 and 0.40 at 1.7B, 4B and 32B). We release registration, code, episodes and analyses.

♻ ☆ InFi-Check: Interpretable and Fine-Grained Fact-Checking of LLMs EMNLP 2026
Yuzhuo Bai, Shuzheng Si, Kangyang Luo, Qingyi Wang, Wenhao Li, Gang Chen, Fanchao Qi, Maosong Sun
Large language models (LLMs) often hallucinate, yet most existing fact-checking methods treat factuality evaluation as a binary classification problem, offering limited interpretability and failing to capture fine-grained error types. In this paper, we introduce InFi-Check, a framework for interpretable and fine-grained fact-checking of LLM outputs. Specifically, we first propose a controlled data synthesis pipeline that generates high-quality data featuring explicit evidence, fine-grained error type labels, justifications, and corrections. Based on this, we further construct large-scale training data and a manually verified benchmark InFi-Check-FG for fine-grained fact-checking of LLM outputs. Building on these high-quality training data, we further propose InFi-Checker, which can jointly provide supporting evidence, classify fine-grained error types, and produce justifications along with corrections. Experiments show that InFi-Checker achieves state-of-the-art performance on InFi-Check-FG and strong generalization across various downstream tasks, significantly improving the utility and trustworthiness of factuality evaluation.
comment: EMNLP 2026
♻ ☆ Auditing Exposure to Harmful Content on TikTok using Multimodal Language Models: A Cross-National, Age-Stratified Study
Hamidreza Saffari, Francesco Pierri
Online video platforms can expose young users to harmful content, but independent audits remain difficult because video annotation is costly and moderation judgments vary across languages. We audit TikTok in France, Italy, and Sweden with sockpuppet accounts representing four age personas (13, 16, 19, 40), collecting 36,971 videos from passive For-You-page scrolling and active sessions that scroll, search for harm keywords, and scroll again. To scale annotation, we validate four multimodal LLMs against native-speaker labels on a 300-video reference set. Gemini 2.5 Flash with eight sampled frames plus text performs best (aggregate kappa = 0.42), at half the per-call cost of native-video upload, and we apply it to a 10% sample for approximately \$50 in total API spend across both modalities. Keyword search returns 35-56% harmful content, a 1.5-7.5x increase over the scrolling baseline in ten of twelve country-age combinations; the spike is temporary and flattens the age differences observed in France and Sweden. Under passive scrolling, Italy has the highest harm rate at every age, with Italian age-19 reaching 48.6%. Overall, MLLM-based auditing offers a scalable approach for cross-national youth-safety audits, while provider safety filters (1.1% refusal rate) under-count the most explicit harms.
comment: 20 pages, 16 figures, 14 tables
♻ ☆ Geometric Latent Reasoning Induces Shorter Generations in LLMs NeurIPS 2026
Shashi Kumar, Yacouba Kaloga, Petr Motlicek, Ina Kodrasi, Andrea Cavallaro
Large language models solve complex problems by generating lengthy chains of explicit reasoning tokens. While effective, this makes reasoning expensive, length-sensitive, and constrained to (discrete) natural language. While latent reasoning offers a continuous alternative, determining useful structures for intermediate latent states is an open challenge. In this paper, we formulate latent reasoning as a geometric path-approximation problem within the model's pretrained token-embedding space. We introduce Geometric Latent Reasoning (GLR), which uses a lightweight transition head to predict iterative direction updates in embedding space. Using textual chain-of-thought traces as anchors, GLR learns to approximate discrete reasoning trajectories while permitting continuous deviations from exact token embeddings. Evaluations on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using Qwen3 models reveal an emergent phenomenon: geometric latent reasoning induces substantially shorter generations without an explicit length objective. By replacing early explicit reasoning with continuous latent steps, models often reach correct answers using substantially fewer total generation steps. These findings suggest that continuous trajectories act as compact intermediate reasoning states, exposing a new tradeoff between latent computation budget, output length, and accuracy. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/idiap/GLR. The project page is available at: https://glr-llm.github.io/.
comment: accepted to NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ MAAM: Anchor-Preserving Compression and Contextual Calibration for Chinese Discriminatory Language Detection EMNLP 2026
Yuxin Fu, Shijing Si
Chinese discriminatory-language detection is challenging because harmful intent is often implicit and context-dependent. We propose MAAM (Myopia--Astigmatism Anchor Mechanism), a lightweight, model-agnostic framework inspired by functional visual blur: rather than preserving every token equally, MAAM retains discrimination-relevant semantic anchors and calibrates them with C--I--S contextual priors (Contextual Tone, Group Identity, and Stance Polarity). We also introduce ChLGBT, to our knowledge the first Chinese LGBT-focused discriminatory-language dataset, with 8,120 manually annotated samples and three ordinal labels: explicit bias, implicit bias, and emotional intensity. Across strong encoder baselines, MAAM improves all three prediction dimensions, with consistent gains in accuracy, F1, Brier score, and expected calibration error. Compared with frontier LLM baselines under zero-shot and few-shot prompting protocols, MAAM remains competitive while offering stronger compactness and stability. These results suggest that interpretable anchor preservation and contextual calibration provide a practical alternative to heavier model scaling for Chinese discriminatory-language assessment.
comment: Accepted at Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. The final published version is available in the ACL Anthology: https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-emnlp.84/
♻ ☆ VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation NeurIPS 2026
Hanxun Huang, Yutao Wu, Qizhou Wang, Silvia Montaña-Niño, Yige Li, Xiang Zheng, Elif Buse Doyuran, Phoebe Matich, Xiao Liu, Xingjun Ma, Sarah Erfani, Christopher Leckie
Large language models (LLMs) have made misinformation inexpensive to produce but not to verify, creating a growing asymmetry in the information ecosystem. Under tight time, labor, and budget constraints, media organizations, platforms, and fact-checkers rely on screening to prioritize which content to verify. We introduce VEX-Bench, a unified benchmark for evaluating the verification complexity of LLM-generated misinformation, as perceived during screening, across models and generation methods. Verification complexity is assessed along multiple dimensions derived from journalistic and fact-checking practices, capturing checkability, harm potential, source credibility signals, imposter legitimacy, and expected verification effort. We define the VEX score as an integrated measure combining elicitation yield and verification complexity to quantify how generated content consumes limited verification capacity. We construct a benchmark spanning two misinformation categories, 6 high-stakes domains, and 60 real-world topics, and evaluate 7 frontier LLMs and 7 generation methods, yielding 5{,}880 articles. We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $α$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. LLMs can generate high-VEX misinformation at 3$\times$ to 169$\times$ lower cost than agent-based verification. Such content is often prioritized during screening, consuming scarce verification resources and introducing a systematic risk of misallocation in resource-constrained verification systems. The code is publicly available in our \href{https://github.com/HanxunH/VEX-Bench}{GitHub repository}.
comment: NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ SocialGym: Evaluating LLM Social Intelligence through Verifiable Multi-Agent Games
Keyu He, Xuhui Zhou, Maarten Sap
Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent social settings where they must cooperate, negotiate, and adapt to other agents. Measuring these social skills is hard because most social interactions offer no objective ground truth. Evaluations often fall back on LLM judges, which are costly, subjective, and noisy. We introduce SocialGym, an environment of 22 multi-agent social games, from matrix games to hidden-role deduction, with verifiable outcomes determined by game rules. We benchmark ten LLMs across all games and roles using an Elo tournament. Our results show that no model is best in every game, and rankings shift across game families and sides. Secret keeping correlates more strongly with theory-of-mind and privacy benchmarks than with general knowledge benchmarks. Half of the models give away their side's secret in Chameleon and Spyfall, and the smallest models are not reliably better than chance at voting for hidden opponents in most hidden-role games. Finally, we examine whether models can improve their play by reflecting on self-play and writing strategy playbooks, finding mixed results across models and games. SocialGym provides verifiable measures for diagnosing LLM social capabilities across settings and roles.
comment: Code and data: https://github.com/Keyu-He/Social_Gym_Spartan
♻ ☆ PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents
Seongjae Kang, Taehyung Yu, Sung Ju Hwang
Customer-service LLM agents must follow organizational policy when acting on a user's behalf. Compliance failures arise from either forbidden actions, such as granting an ineligible change, or omitted procedural requirements, such as identification or confirmation. Runtime safeguards can intervene on risky actions, but action-local checks do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. Workflow-following systems support prescribed process execution, but primarily target workflow completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior. PolicyGuide instead compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. From persisted graph state, the verifier reconciles open requests and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Across the $τ^2$-bench airline, retail, and telecom domains with a GPT 5.4 agent and verifier, PolicyGuide raises mean $\mathrm{Pass}^4$ from $0.42$ to $0.62$, with the largest gain on telecom ($0.19$ to $0.61$), the most workflow-structured domain. The same workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Complementary evaluations find the lowest observed attack-success rate under adversarial users and the strongest procedural compliance in an independently validated workflow-level audit.
comment: 26 pages, 14 figures, including appendices
♻ ☆ PolicyGuard: A Dialogue-Grounded Sub-Agent Verifier for Policy Adherence in LLM Agents
Seongjae Kang, Taehyung Yu, Sung Ju Hwang
LLM agents handle user requests on behalf of organizations through tool calls and must follow the company policies stated in their system prompts. Prior work approaches this as a safeguarding problem -- external checks that block non-compliant agent actions. We argue that policy adherence is broader: real workflows unfold across many turns, require explicit user confirmation and prerequisite reads, and hinge on dialogue rather than on any single argument value. We introduce PolicyGuard, a sub-agent verifier that shares the agent's view of the dialogue, reasons over the policy in context, and returns actionable remediation. On $τ^2$-bench airline across GPT 5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 2.5 Pro, PolicyGuard improves $\mathrm{Pass}^4$, the fraction of tasks successful in all four trials, by +12.0 / +6.0 / +12.0 pp; pooled paired tests support an overall cross-vendor effect. We further evaluate PolicyGuard on the full retail and telecom base splits, covering all three $τ^2$-bench customer-service domains. Further analyses show that PolicyGuard improves reliability beyond agent self-checking, catches more policy violations with fewer blocks than argument-level guards, and preserves its refusal accuracy under three adversarial probes.
comment: 21 pages. Updated manuscript with expanded cross-domain evaluation and analyses
♻ ☆ Scaling Inherently Interpretable Language Models
GuideLabs, Andreas Madsen, Aya Abdelsalam Ismail, Giang Nguyen, Isaac Plant, Muawiz Chaudhary, Nathaniel Monson, Saqib Azim, Zhichen Guo, Julius Adebayo
Interpretability is often treated as a tax on capability: language models are trained as opaque systems, then explained after the fact, with methods whose reliability is difficult to establish. In this work, we challenge this premise. Rather than reverse-engineering a model, we make interpretability a constraint of the training pipeline, optimized alongside the language modeling objective. Across three orders of magnitude of compute, on both autoregressive and diffusion language models, interpretability scales with capability rather than against it. Surprisingly, model representations become more disentangled and aligned with human-understandable concepts with scale. We instantiate the training-time recipe with Steerling-8B, a diffusion language model with a causal attention mask. For any group of generated tokens, Steerling-8B attributes the output to relevant input tokens, human-understandable concepts, and training data. This enables closed-loop intervention: diagnose an output through its concept or feature attribution, retrieve similar training data, and correct the behavior through concept steering without retraining. Steerling-8B remains competitive with open peer models trained on substantially 2-16x more compute, suggesting a different scaling paradigm: interpretability can be designed into training, and it improves with scale.
♻ ☆ Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
Vladimir Beskorovainyi
Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release has higher point accuracy in all fourteen cells, by up to 0.24; eleven differences survive a Holm correction and eight have a label-level interval that excludes zero. Two runs trained by mistake without the transliterated label forms stay at the earlier release's level on jargon. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation. On abbreviations and opaque codes the augmented release gives no usable gain: on the 17 abbreviations unrelated to training it is lower (-0.060, Holm p=0.017), and on opaque codes it stays near chance once labels related to training options are removed. With eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points; one additive bias per option, fitted on half of the rows, narrows these to -3.4 and +1.4 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

♻ ☆ What Simple Readouts Miss in Continuous Language Diffusion
Zhicheng Du, Lan Ma
How much of a learned decoder can a simple readout preserve? On generated ELF and AURORA states, token-wise affine maps recover $97.17\%$ and $95.74\%$ of native lexical decisions. Contextual computation has already produced these states; only the terminal readout is simplified. The remaining disagreements matter beyond their count: equal-count rare-first and low-native-margin-first repairs have opposing pooled evaluator effects in both interfaces. On conditional summarization, rare-first improves reference similarity, while source consistency remains unresolved. Score accounting locates part of the benefit on unchanged text despite increased unigram cost, without identifying rarity as a cause. Repeatable repair effects do not ensure prediction transfer: a frozen predictor improves on two ELF checkpoints but fails on a distilled student. A separate task-fitted selector improves BERTScore over random selection by $0.261$ points on 256 fresh articles at a $50\%$ native-call budget; all-native decoding remains higher-scoring and acceleration is unestablished. Compressed and directional interface tests further distinguish fitting-state coverage, native decisions, and soft inputs. Together, the results motivate testing a simplification at three levels: preserved decisions, output consequences, and computational savings. Native decisions are fidelity targets, not semantic truth.
♻ ☆ Contrastive-Difference CKA Reveals Concept-Specific Structural Alignment Across Language Model Architectures ACML 2026
Xueping Gao
Do language models encode the same prompted concepts in structurally compatible ways, beyond generic similarity induced by shared questions? We study contrastive-difference centered kernel alignment ($\mathrm{CKA}_Δ$), which compares per-question activation differences between opposing concept instructions. A matched same-concept versus cross-concept comparison separates the question of concept-conditioned structure from the magnitude of representational similarity. Across four checkpoints and eight personality-related traits, a fixed-final-layer analysis gives mean same- and cross-trait $\mathrm{CKA}_Δ$ of 0.7259 and 0.6828. Trait-label randomization detects correspondence conditional on this model and prompt set ($p=1/10001$, one-sided), but a model-and-trait-weighted 95% interval for the difference is $[-0.0330,0.1017]$, limiting broader generalization. Strict question-group holdouts retain high same-trait linear recoverability. More stringently, maps and preprocessing fitted on seven traits transfer a source polarity classifier for the eighth trait to handwritten test questions: mean affine and orthogonal accuracies are 88.10% and 88.57%, versus 47.70% for shuffled pairing. Performance varies substantially across traits and model directions. Synthetic controls show why moderate CKA and high affine accuracy alone do not establish functional equivalence. The results support a scoped diagnostic of concept-specific structure and held-out linear recoverability; they do not establish universal invariance or a robust advantage over raw CKA across architectures.
comment: Accepted at ACML 2026 (Conference Track). 13-page main paper plus 18-page supplementary material. Revised theoretical statements and statistical analysis; added grouped holdouts and concept-held-out transfer evaluation; narrowed claims
♻ ☆ Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers
Wenhan Ma, Hailin Zhang, Liang Zhao, Yifan Song, Yudong Wang, Zhifang Sui, Fuli Luo
Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial approach for enhancing the capabilities of large language models. However, in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the routing mechanism often introduces instability, even leading to catastrophic RL training collapse. We analyze the training-inference consistency of MoE models and identify a notable discrepancy in routing behaviors between the two phases. Moreover, even under identical conditions, the routing framework can yield divergent expert selections across repeated forward passes. To address this foundational inconsistency, we propose Rollout Routing Replay (R3), a method that records routing distributions from the inference engine and replays them during training. R3 significantly reduces training-inference policy KL divergence and mitigates extreme discrepancies without compromising training speed. Extensive experiments on various settings confirm that R3 succeeds in stabilizing RL training, preventing collapse and outperforming methods such as GSPO and TIS. We believe this work can offer a new solution for stabilizing RL in MoE models.
♻ ☆ Are Multilingual Models Actually Improving? Revisiting Cross-Lingual Transfer
Prasoon Bajpai, Eleftheria Briakou, Colin Cherry, Preethi Jyothi, Vihari Piratla
Cross-lingual transfer is a model's ability to generalize capabilities from well-represented source languages to under-represented target languages. Existing measures of a model's transfer strength conflate improvements in transfer with general improvements to accuracy in the source language. We advocate for an alternate metric that reliably captures transfer strength called Hardness Adjusted Transfer (HAT) Score, and use it to derive multiple insights on factors influencing transfer strength. Our analysis across twenty diverse language models and three popular mainstream multilingual benchmarks argues that 1) transfer in small models is not broken, 2) we are making slower than expected progress in cross-lingual transfer with model size, and 3) we have made clear progress over time.
♻ ☆ A Channel-Boosted Multi-Agent System with Iterative Consultation for Document Sensitivity Classification
Aleesha Zainab, Asifullah Khan, Muhammad Ahmed Khalid, Faheem Ullah Khan
Organizations in critical national infrastructure sectors must assess heterogeneous documents for sensitivity before routing or storage. Manual assessment is slow, inconsistent, and unscalable. Extending our prior leakage-controlled benchmark, BERT established the top single-encoder baseline (89.14% accuracy, 89.33% F1-score under 5-fold cross-validation on the Strategic 16K corpus). However, transformer baselines suffer from a structural limitation: fixed input length truncation discards evidence beyond the retained window-precisely where sensitive cables tend to be longest. We present Channel-Boosted MAS (CB-MAS) and instantiate it as IC-MAS (Iterative Consultation Multi-Agent System) to solve this without long-context computational costs. A Channel Critic Agent learns document-adaptive trust weights governing Gated Channel Boosting between two first-window encoders, while paired Consultation Agents iteratively exchange belief states to reconcile evidence from the beginning and end of long documents. IC-MAS holds computation constant regardless of document length by reconciling fixed windows in a compact representation space. Ablation studies show critic-controlled Channel Boosting provides the bulk of accuracy gains, while consultation recovers recall without precision collapse. Critic-Controlled Gated Channel Boosting with Max-Pool fusion and Blackboard Adaptive Consultation achieves 90.72% accuracy, 91.23% F1-score, 92.01% sensitive recall, and 90.46% sensitive precision, using about 54% less average computation than a fixed-round baseline. Gains over the single-encoder baseline are statistically significant (McNemar's test, p less than 0.000001; paired t-test). We include LIME/SHAP explainability, multi-agent evaluation, and an honest accounting of limitations.
comment: 40 pages , 14 figures
♻ ☆ Hint-Guided Diversified Policy Optimization for LLM Reasoning
Zhiyu Cao, Kaixin Wu, Mingjie Zhong, Peifeng Li, Can Ye, Qiaoming Zhu
Recent developments in Large Language Models (LLMs) have showcased impressive reasoning capabilities, with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) being a promising enhancement strategy. However, existing reward mechanisms are constrained to the outcome-level correctness and lack explicit signals to guide the model to consider diverse solutions. In contrast, human problem solving typically involves evaluating multiple potential approaches and selecting the most reliable solution, a cognitive process that current RLVR frameworks do not explicitly incentivize. Inspired by this, we propose Hint-Guided Diversified Policy Optimization (HDPO), allowing the model to first list all potential candidate solution outlines as hints and then select the most reliable one for further reasoning. HDPO comprises two stages of Cold Start for Structured Reasoning and Hint-Guided Diversified Reinforcement Learning to incentivize the model to generate diverse and reliable solutions following the ``propose-select-think'' trajectory. Experimental results show that HDPO effectively boosts LLM reasoning and enhances the diversity of candidate solutions as well as the LLM's ability to identify reliable solutions.
♻ ☆ An Enigma of Artificial Reason: Investigating the Production-Evaluation Gap in Large Reasoning Models NeurIPS 2026
Mingzhong Sun, Teresa Yeo, Armando Solar-Lezama, Tan Zhi-Xuan
Studies of human reasoning have shown that people are typically stronger at evaluating reasoning than producing it from scratch. In contrast, large reasoning models (LRMs) are trained to excel at producing long chains of reasoning to solve complex problems. How then do LRMs perform at evaluating reasons? We investigate this with the Valid-Answer-Invalid-Reasoning (VAIR) dataset: math problems and solutions with trivial reasoning flaws but valid answers, designed to isolate reasoning evaluation from the confound of reasoning production. Unlike humans, who we find are only 6% worse at grading than solving such problems, we find a substantial production-evaluation gap in LRMs: frontier models score as low as 52% when evaluating VAIR solutions, despite near-perfect solution production. Why this enigma? Through chain-of-thought (CoT) analysis, we find evidence of an answer confirmation bias: LRMs often produce then check for the correct answer instead of carefully verifying each step, fabricating rationalizations even when noticing anomalous reasoning. Linear probes corroborate this, showing that while LRM activations encode some representation of valid reasoning, they fail to robustly represent VAIR solutions as invalid. Causal patching of the final answer's representations causes LRM verdicts and activations to flip at substantial rates, demonstrating that answer validity is a causal factor in models' confirmation biases. These findings indicate an outstanding limitation in dominant approaches to reasoning training, which incentivize LRMs to produce and confirm reasoning towards correct answers, but not to robustly evaluate the underlying reasons
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables (Appendix: 19 pages, 13 figures, 3 tables) Proceedings to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
♻ ☆ MJ: Multi-turn LLM Jailbreaking via Decomposed Credit Assignment
Junyoung Park, Namgyu Park, Sechan Lee, Yoon-Chan Jhi, Jihoon Cho, Sangdon Park
Modern large language models (LLMs) operate in interactive multi-turn settings, making multi-turn jailbreaking a realistic threat model and an important setting for automated red teaming. A core challenge in learning multi-turn jailbreak attackers is credit assignment: different turns contribute differently to the final outcome, yet existing learning signals are often too coarse to identify their individual contributions. We propose decomposed credit GRPO (DC-GRPO), a unified turn-level credit assignment framework for Group Relative Policy Optimization in multi-turn jailbreak learning. DC-GRPO assigns a separate group-relative learning signal to each turn by combining immediate and future credit, avoiding the credit misassignment induced by broadcasting a single trajectory-level score across the dialogue. We instantiate this framework with static and dynamic weighting rules that differ in how the two credit sources are balanced while sharing the same turn-level structure. Across four victim LLMs and three benchmarks, DC-GRPO achieves up to 98.26% average ASR_5@3, substantially outperforming the state-of-the-art methods, including SEMA (86.58%) and TROJail (86.23%), demonstrating the effectiveness of our turn-level group-relative credit assignment. ♻ ☆ PathXAI: Evidence-guided structured pathology reporting by transferable tissue segmentation
Zhaorui Tan, Jun Aun Tan, Weixiang Zhong, Xiaoxi Wang, Tan Pan, Xingdong Xue, Li Liu, Jing Zhang, Jing Zhang, Weimiao Yu
Pathology reporting requires translating tissue observations across regions and slides into specific diagnoses and supporting morphological descriptions. However, the use of explicit tissue-composition measurements to guide H&E-based report generation remains underexplored. Thus, we developed PathXAI, which combines segmentation-derived tissue information with H&E images and optional domain knowledge to guide diagnostic reasoning, targeted reinspection and structured report writing. Its segmentation component exceeded baselines in mean Dice on internal and external tests. In automated report evaluation on 1,200 public and 151 private cases, PathXAI achieved higher agreement with reference diagnoses and documented morphology than the H&E-based comparators. On the public evaluation cohort, PathXAI-Report exceeded Qwen + H&E in cancer family match rate by 4.4 percentage points and in finding F1 by 5.7 percentage points. PathXAI generates evidence-linked reports with a self-hosted pretrained vision-language model, without updating its weights.

♻ ☆ Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
Adil Amin
Scaling exponents of neural dimensionality are read as properties of the code, and used to compare representations and benchmark models against cortex. Yet one recording of 11,311 mouse V1 neurons gives 0.25, 0.30 or 0.35, depending only on how it is subsampled. We show that such an exponent measures the population and the probe together. We split it exactly into a floor, which random subsets of the same sizes give, and a shift, which a declared axis of stimulus classes adds. The usual random-subsample exponent is almost all floor. Stimulus direction lifts the exponent in every grating recording by reading both symmetry sectors of the code: orientation, which repeats every half turn, and direction, which does not. The lift lives in trial-to-trial fluctuations that differ between directions, while the class means, which linear decoders read, pull it down. Two measured terms, how much the classes' fluctuations overlap and how the means sit against them, account for the shift. They give its sign where it changes: in Allen Neuropixels recordings, whose class means mostly raise the exponent, and in macaque V1. In an XY lattice whose classes stay on one orbit, temperature flips the sign as the two terms say, and in GPT-2 the shift ranks the indirect-object circuit's name-mover and backup heads. Reported with its path, its floor and its shift, an exponent says how much structure a probe finds and what carries it. Our open tool, rung, reports all three for any labelled neural recording or language-model layer: https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom
comment: Accepted at NeurReps 2026 (Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research. 48 pages. Code, data and the rung tool: https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom. Five-minute talk: https://youtu.be/S4kUtP37KLM
♻ ☆ Pause and Reflect: Conformal Aggregation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning NeurIPS 2026
Yu Gu, Zijun Yu, Vahid Partovi Nia, Masoud Asgharian
Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with self-consistency improves performance by aggregating multiple sampled reasoning paths. In this setting, correctness is no longer tied to a single reasoning trace but to the aggregation rule over a pool of candidate paths, making aggregation uncertainty the central challenge. This issue is critical where confidently incorrect answers are far more costly than abstentions. We introduce a conformal procedure for CoT reasoning that directly addresses aggregation uncertainty. Our approach replaces majority voting with weighted score aggregation over reasoning paths and calibrates an abstention rule using conformal risk control. This approach leads to finite-sample guarantees on the confident-error rate--the probability that the system answers and is wrong. We further identify score separability as the key condition under which abstention provably improves selective accuracy, and derive closed-form expressions that predict accuracy gains from calibration data alone. The method is fully inference-time, and requires no retraining. Across four benchmarks, four open-source models, and three score classes, realized confident-error rates are consistent with the prescribed targets up to calibration-split and test-set variability. Our method achieves $90.1\%$ selective accuracy on GSM8K by abstaining on fewer than $5\%$ of problems, compared with $82.3\%$ accuracy under majority voting and $87.4\%$ under score-weighted voting without abstention, while conformal risk control keeps the expected rate of confidently wrong answers below $10\%$.
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version. Code: https://github.com/Zijun-Y/conformal-cot-aggregation
♻ ☆ Who Pays More for Safety? Measuring the Disparate Cost of Safety Alignment across Languages EMNLP 2026
Chanwoong Yoon, Jungsoo Park, Alan Ritter
Safety alignment helps models adhere to human values, but it often reduces response utility. We ask a critical but understudied question: Does safety alignment impose the cost equally across language groups? To answer this, we introduce a rigorous protocol to measure the utility loss imposed solely by safety alignment, which we term Safety Cost. Through direct pairwise comparisons between safety-aligned models and their unaligned counterparts, we find a systematic inequity: non-English users consistently bear a higher Safety Cost than English users. We further identify three underlying patterns. First, multiple languages lie in a double-penalty zone, experiencing both weaker safety protection and larger utility loss. Second, certain languages exhibit apparent utility gains that are in fact a consequence of safety filters failing to engage. Third, even high-resource languages pay a larger Safety Cost than English to reach the same level of safety. We show that these disparities arise from both explicit refusals and implicit qualitative differences across multiple dimensions. By accurately measuring the disparate effects of safety alignment, our findings expose a systematic disparity in current safety alignment practices.
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. Code: https://github.com/cwyoon-99/who-pays-more-for-safety
♻ ☆ DynEdit: Dynamic Entropy-Guided Sequential Editing for Large Language Models NeurIPS 2026
Jinhu Fu, Yan Bai, Yihang Lou, Li Sun, Jiahong Wu, Xiangxiang Chu, Sen Su
Knowledge editing aims to update outdated or incorrect knowledge in large language models without full retraining. Existing parameter-editing methods remain limited for long-sequence knowledge: single-point editors provide insufficient coverage for extended targets, while fixed chunk-based editors distribute editing effort uniformly across rigid predefined windows, failing to prioritize difficult, information-dense tokens. In this work, we show that token entropy is closely associated with both editing difficulty and semantic importance: high-entropy regions are harder to edit and often contain key factual content. Motivated by this observation, we propose DynEdit, a dynamic framework for long-sequence knowledge editing. DynEdit uses token-level entropy to guide non-uniform sliding, increasing the coverage of difficult high-entropy regions, and further applies entropy-guided token-level optimization to strengthen updates on information-dense tokens within each editing window. Experiments on three benchmarks and two backbone models show that DynEdit consistently outperforms competitive baselines across diverse long-form editing settings, achieving gains of up to +14.0 BLEU points on challenging paraphrase queries and near-saturated semantic scores on several diverse knowledge domains.
comment: Accepted by main conference of NeurIPS 2026 (poster)
♻ ☆ StateRAG: Typed State Contracts for Complex Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Miaohe Niu, Pengxiang Li, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
Complex retrieval-augmented generation requires evidence retrieval and control over what to retrieve next, which paths to explore, whether evidence is sufficient, and which intermediate results to retain. Existing RAG paradigms encode these decisions through method-specific model contexts, traversal procedures, verification signals, and memory. We introduce StateRAG, which represents retrieval control as a typed state external to the final reader. The state records the query plan, typed traversal path, candidate evidence, verification verdict, and reusable artifacts, with defined field semantics and designated update sources. Ordered role operators propose field values, and the controller validates and commits accepted proposals. A one-time compact-evidence check may select Bypass. Otherwise, the controller combines the committed verdict with the remaining budget to select Release, Revise, or Fallback. The final reader is invoked only after a terminal action and at most once per query. Among the evaluated methods, StateRAG achieves the best score on 10 of 11 reported quality metrics across LongBench, QASPER, and DocVQA. Its LongBench macro-average EM and F1 exceed ReAct by 6.3 and 6.1 percentage points, and its largest task-level gain is 9.8 F1 points on MuSiQue. Under normalized model-size weighting, StateRAG records lower mean LLM-token use per query than ReAct across all five workloads. In a matched LongBench control, the typed, role-owned carrier exceeds a free-form shared carrier by 1.3, 2.2, and 3.0 percentage points in macro EM, F1, and accuracy, with 6.2% lower mean RET. Removing TAM, MARS, or SMP lowers every reported LongBench and QASPER ablation metric.
♻ ☆ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
Henrique Schechter Vera, Sahil Dua, Jovan Andonov, Sara Smoot, Sebastian Russo, Ivan Llanos, Max Matveev, Jae Hyeon Yoo, Kat Black, Shih-Cheng Huang, Josiah Aklilu, Maarten Grootendorst, Omar Sanseviero, Chandramouli Amarnath, Ian Ballantyne, Zhe Li, Daniel Salz, Ibrahim Alabdulmohsin, Ilya Philippov, Kristen Quan, Glenn Cameron, Edouard Yvinec, Luciano Martins, Doug Reid, Sindhu Raghuram Panyam, Weiyi Wang, Hengxuan Ying, Madhuri Shanbhogue, Tanmaya Dabral, Shanfeng Zhang, Juyeong Ji, Renjie Wu, Joe Zou, Xu Chen, Yunan Zhang, Yu-Hui Chen, Matthew Soulanille, Vinod Mamillapalli, Yi-Chun Kuo, Wai Hon Law, Matt Kreileder, Alice Zheng, Suril Shah, Mogan Shieh, Pooja Consul, Alberto Montes, Andreas Hess, Andres Sevilla, Babak Samari, Brendan McCloskey, Brian Potetz, Daniel Cer, Dilip Kumar Margam, Feodor Beloborodov, Georgios Kathareios, Gustavo Hernández Ábrego, Hesen Zhang, Ji Ma, Jianan Lu, Jiaxing Wu, Keegan Mosley, Paul Suganthan, Rui Meng, Shen Gao, Shengcao Cao, Wing Lowe, Yi-Ting Chen, Yichang Chen, Zhongli Ding, Kendra Byrne, Cormac Brick, Olivier Lacombe, Qin Yin, Tris Warkentin, Armand Joulin, Tom Duerig, Mojtaba Seyedhosseini
We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. ♻ ☆ GLINT: Sparsely Gated Vision-Language Alignment for Fine-Grained Radiology Representations NeurIPS 2026
Jonggwon Park, Seongeun Lee, Junhyun Park, Hannah Yun, Hyunwoong Kim, Sohyun Jeong, Hyewon Kang, Byungmu Yoon, Kyoyun Choi
Vision-language models (VLMs) for radiology have emerged as a scalable paradigm by leveraging image-report pairs naturally produced in clinical workflows. However, this pairing reveals a mismatch in scale: each finding occupies only a small region of the image, yet supervision is provided only at the global image-report level. This poses a central challenge: prior approaches spread weight densely across all patches rather than concentrating on the sparse subset relevant to a given query. To address this, we present GLINT (Gated Language-Image alignmeNT), a framework that models this sparse correspondence. On the alignment side, we introduce Sparsely Gated Alignment, a novel architecture in which a sigmoid gate over a separate gate embedding space activates only the patches relevant to each textual query, yielding sparsity. On the representation side, we add Dense Feature Regularization, which anchors the trainable encoder's intermediate features to a frozen self-supervised learning (SSL) teacher, preserving the fine-grained patch features that the gate relies on. The same recipe applies to both 2D chest X-ray (CXR) and 3D chest computed tomography (CT), built with DINOv3 and V-JEPA 2.1, respectively. GLINT enables zero-shot classification, grounding, and segmentation from free-text queries, and to our knowledge is the first to demonstrate zero-shot segmentation on 3D CT volumes without mask supervision. Notably, the most pronounced gains arise on zero-shot grounding and segmentation, where sparse, query-specific localization is required, consistent with our design intent. In downstream evaluation, GLINT outperforms both SSL encoders and medical VLMs on classification, report generation, and segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/deepnoid-ai/GLINT.

☆ Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
Haozhi Yuan, Handong Li, Yifan Zhang, Qianshan Wei
Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.
☆ World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
Heng Fang, Zehui Guo, Yuehan Zhang, Mingyang Du, Dingkang Liang, Xiang Bai
Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript

☆ Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization NeurIPS 2026
Zhaoying Pan, Yipei Wang, Shenyu Lu, Xiaoqian Wang
Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation.

☆ Beyond Modality Preference: Controlling Multimodal Arbitration under Modality Conflict in MLLMs WACV 2027
Zhaoying Pan, Shenyu Lu, Jun Hui Wong, Junyi Chai, Xiaoqian Wang
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) integrate information across modalities, but become unreliable when those modalities disagree. Under conflicting inputs, MLLMs may favor modalities that are not the most reliable for the task, thus motivating inference-time control of modality arbitration. We identify a small set of attention heads, termed arbitration heads, that causally influence whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight, training-free intervention that biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time. The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalize across settings, and steering them enables effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks. Our findings identify an effective control mechanism to align MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.
comment: WACV 2027
☆ Grasping the Future: Joint 3D Hand-Object Forecasting From Internet Videos
Rustin Soraki, Matthew Wallingford, Ryan Aby, Brandon Chee, Jason Ren, Ali Farhadi, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Roozbeh Mottaghi
To interact with an object, we need to anticipate both how it will move and how our hands should move with it. Human videos capture these relationships across everyday activities, offering a natural source for learning to predict future interactions. Learning from them requires recovering motion from completed interactions and using it to anticipate what could happen next. We present $\textit{Grasping-the-Future}$, a unified generative model of joint 3D hand-object motion, including wrist motion, finger articulation, and object position and orientation. Through masked spatiotemporal completion and flow matching, we train a single model for several prediction tasks: forecasting future interactions, predicting hand motion given object motion or vice versa, generating both trajectories toward a desired final object pose, and completing partially observed interactions. We explicitly model hand-object relations and incorporate contact constraints to help preserve grasp relationships during motion. To obtain 3D supervision from internet videos, we develop a scalable pipeline that combines pretrained perception models with joint geometric optimization to reconstruct completed interactions. We combine these recovered trajectories with annotated interaction datasets as training data for all tasks. We demonstrate strong performance across all tasks, outperforming released forecasters on datasets with 3D annotations. Moreover, we show geometric and physical plausibility of the predicted trajectories by retargeting them to a robotic embodiment. Videos are available at https://grasping-the-future.github.io.
☆ Click3R: Interactive Stereo 3D Reconstruction with Sparse Correspondence Clicks NeurIPS 2026
Hao Gu, Jin Yao, Zezhou Cheng
Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://uva-computer-vision-lab.github.io/click3r/
☆ SWAM: Scaling World Action Models with Cross-Modal Alignment
Yu Zhou, Xinyuan Xia, Xuankun Yang, Yinghao Yang, Wendi Chen, Bowen Liu, Jianhan Ma, Weicheng Duan, Jun Lv, Cewu Lu, Yanwei Li
World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.
☆ AI-based characterization of lymphoid structures and the tumor microenvironment reveals lower mature tertiary lymphoid structures, lymph-node follicles, and plasma cells after neoadjuvant therapy in lung squamous cell carcinoma
Arne Schmidt, Justin Nieder, Cornelius Boehm, Julika Ribbat-Idel, Marius Teodorescu, Marie-Lisa Eich, Simon Schallenberg, Gabriel Dernbach, Katja Lingelbach, Miriam Haegele, Timo Milbich, Adam Narai, Maria Stoelben, Hans Pinckaers, Lukas Ruff, Kai Standvoss, Christian Watermann, Christiane Kuempers, Sven Perner, Verena Sailer, Jasmin Tiebach, Torsten Goldmann, Sebastian Marwitz, Johannes Braegelmann, Frederick Klauschen, Marija Pezer, Rosemarie Krupar

How this loco-regional axis differs between neoadjuvant-treated and therapy-naive tumors is poorly defined. Aignostics Atlas H&E Tissue Analysis (HETA) models quantified cell densities per tissue compartment and cell-cell co-localization; a dedicated deep-learning model validated against pathologist annotations detected TLS and SLS and graded their maturity. In neoLUSC tumors, stromal plasma cell density was 72% (p=0.004) and stromal lymphocyte density 48% (p=0.015) lower than in naivLUSC; macrophages and granulocytes did not differ significantly. Total and immature TLS did not differ, whereas mature TLS in the tumor (p=0.034) and mature SLS in the tumor-distal lymph node (p=0.003) were lower in neoLUSC patients. Peri-TLS plasma cell density correlated with tumor lymphocyte density in naivLUSC (rho=0.54, p=0.017) but not in neoLUSC tumors (rho=0.07). In the validation cohort, stromal plasma cell density (HR 0.69, p=0.011) and lymphocyte-plasma cell co-localization (HR 0.66, p=0.004) were associated with longer survival, and neoadjuvant status with shorter survival (HR 1.50, p=0.026). ☆ What kills $v$-prediction? A Patch-wise PCA Perspective on Pixel-Space Flow Matching NeurIPS 2026
Tianze Luo, Haofeng Huang, Yuan Yao
Latent Diffusion Models dominate generative modeling but face two-stage training complexity and the inherent reconstruction limits of pre-trained autoencoders. Pixel-space Flow Matching offers a simplified end-to-end alternative yet often encounters training difficulties when using the standard $v$-prediction objective. Recent research attributes this difficulty to the off-manifold nature of noised targets, motivating a shift toward $x$-prediction. In this paper, we investigate this explanation through patch-wise Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and identify a bandwidth bottleneck. The velocity in minor components is largely determined by the raw noisy input, requiring deep backbones to preserve information that competes with principal-component modeling. Through controlled experiments and representation analysis, we further examine why $x$-prediction remains effective: its parameterization provides a raw-input bypass, while its learned input representation can spontaneously concentrate on principal directions. Under low-rank observations, our analysis of the induced flow characterizes $x$-prediction as an implicit conditional-mean decoder, reconstructing discarded components from the retained information. These observations motivate the Raw-injected Transformer (RiT), which combines a lightweight raw-conditioned decoder with an output-side shortcut to separate semantic modeling from raw-state propagation. Our method restores effective $v$-prediction and achieves competitive performance on ImageNet $256\times256$, providing a perspective on the interaction between prediction objectives and architectural bandwidth.

☆ 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling NeurIPS 2026
Aarya Bhave, Anushka Ajay Bhave
Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $Φ$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.

☆ Complementarity-Driven Dual-Teacher Hierarchical Alignment for Zero-Shot EEG-to-Image Retrieval
Lukun Wu, Jie Li, Ziqi Ren, Ruiyang Xia, Yan Gao, Xinbo Gao
Decoding visual information from EEG is central to brain--computer interfaces and brain-inspired intelligence, and contrastive alignment with pretrained vision foundation models (VFMs) has become the dominant paradigm. However, existing methods align EEG solely with CLIP-family VFMs, leaving hierarchical visual information in neural responses under-exploited. To address this gap, we formulate a mechanism-paradigm correspondence view linking hierarchical visual processing (from appearance to semantics) to the complementary biases of cross-paradigm VFMs, with image-only models (e.g., DINO) and image--text models (e.g., CLIP) capturing distinct facets of this hierarchy. Guided by this view, we propose the Dual-Teacher Hierarchical Alignment (DTHA) framework. Concretely, a shared EEG encoder is supervised by frozen multi-blur CLIP and shallow DINOv2 teachers via dual-branch contrastive alignment, so each branch fully supervises the visual cues it emphasizes. A fused-retrieval objective learns adaptive weights to combine their complementary visual representations for zero-shot EEG-to-image retrieval. For the shared EEG encoder, we introduce the Attentive Modulated Scalp-Pattern Bank Encoder (AMSPBE), combining temporo-spatial attention with a learnable scalp-pattern bank for accurate, interpretable visual feature extraction, while modeling regional temporal dynamics and filter-bank topographies. On THINGS-EEG zero-shot retrieval, DTHA achieves 92.4% Top-1 accuracy, exceeding prior state of the art by 12.4 percentage points. Spatial, spectral, and representational-similarity analyses, together with THINGS-MEG evaluation, validate DTHA's effectiveness, biological plausibility, and cross-modality generalization. This complementarity-driven perspective shows that supervision from cross-paradigm VFMs enables more complete extraction of hierarchical visual information from brain activity.

☆ Anchor Behavior, Not Parameters: Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning with a Single Shared Prompt WACV 2027
Duy-Cuong Bui, Trung-Anh Dang, Vincent Nguyen, Duc V. Le, Ngoc-Son Vu
Prompt-based continual learning adapts a frozen pre-trained vision transformer by tuning a small set of prompt tokens. Recently, one-prompt methods which share one single prompt across all tasks make this paradigm maximally parameter efficient. The open question is how a shared prompt can keep the knowledge of old classes while being updated for new ones. Existing methods protect old knowledge in parameter space, where they freeze task-specific prompts, expand new components, or sparsely gate which tokens receive gradients. However, this method sacrifices plasticity, yet the drift it still permits in shared tokens can corrupt the prompt's function on past classes. What must be preserved is the prompt's behavior. We propose TEA-Prompt, which couples (i) a token evaluation module that assigns each prompt token a continuous, input-conditional relevance score injected into the attention logits, softly specializing tokens across tasks without discarding any of them, and (ii) an attention-behavior anchoring loss that constrains each token's attention output around class-specific query regions using only compact Gaussian query statistics without stored old images, weighted by the token's past relevance. Anchoring the attention value allows the parameters to continue updating freely, as long as their interaction remains unchanged. TEA-Prompt achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with markedly lower forgetting on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 with only 0.38M parameters. Selecting an effective cover photo is a critical yet understudied problem in visual merchandising for e-commerce marketplaces. On Airbnb, hosts upload many photos depicting different rooms, amenities, and points of interest, but must manually choose a single static cover photo that is reused across heterogeneous product surfaces. This creates substantial challenges: over 90\% of listing photos have no engagement labels, leading to a severe cold-start regime; guest preferences vary across surfaces and search intents, and visually captivating photos may be semantically misaligned with the underlying listing. We evaluate OptiCover through extensive offline studies and multiple online experiments across HomePage, and Search surfaces. OptiCover is now deployed in production and performs tens of millions of photo swaps daily. Online results show a 1.5\% engagement lift on the HomePage and a 0.35\% increase in bookers on Search, generating millions of dollars in incremental revenue. Our findings suggest that action-space shaping and semantic constraints are primary drivers of performance.
